t: Fell in battle, or made war?
p: Alexandrinus says only that Nicanor had "made war"; the other Greek copies say he fell. The Plain English Translation follows them.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), in Swete's notes; Sinaiticus (ℵ), whose corrector wrote a form of the verb "fell" over the first scribe's slip; Vulgate; KJV
readings.orig: εποιησεν] επισεν ℵ* (επεισ. ℵc.a) επεσεν V … πολεμω ℵ εν πολ. V
readings.en: Nicanor and his forces had fallen in battle

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐποίησεν Νικάνωρ καὶ αἱ δυνάμεις αὐτοῦ πόλεμον
readings.en: Nicanor and his forces had made war

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. Nicanor died in the battle just told (7:43), so news that he "had made war" is not news. Sinaiticus's first scribe wrote επισεν, which could be a slip for either verb; its corrector's επεισ(εν) points to "fell", and Venetus has ἔπεσεν with "in battle". The forms ἔπεσεν and ἐποίησεν look alike, and A's reading is best taken as a copying slip. The Latin (cecidit, Vulgate 9:1) and the KJV ("were slain") also have "fell".

a: Our time has drawn near. Let us die
t: "Our time has come" or "if our time has come"?
p: Alexandrinus makes Judas sure that his hour has come; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV make it a condition.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ἤγγικεν ὁ καιρὸς ἡμῶν, καὶ ἀποθάνωμεν
readings.en: and our time has drawn near, and let us die
readings.plain: Our time has drawn near. Let us die

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (si appropiavit); KJV ("if our time be come")
readings.orig: ηγγι κεν] pr ει ℵV (Swete's line break kept)
readings.en: if our time has drawn near, let us die
readings.plain: If our time has drawn near, let us die

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus, the base text. Its "and" before "let us die" is awkward Greek, and ℵ and V smooth the sentence by adding "if" (they also drop the second "and"). That smoothing is the likelier change. The difference matters: in A Judas knows he will die; in the other copies he is ready to die if it comes to that.

p: Sinaiticus and Venetus, with the Latin, say they remembered their brother's blood: he had been killed.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ἐμνήσθησαν Ἰωάννου τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτῶν
readings.en: and they remembered John their brother

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as first written (ℵ*) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (recordati sunt sanguinis Joannis)
readings.orig: εμνησθησαν] + του αιματος ℵ* (improb) ℵc.a⁽ᵛⁱᵈ⁾; postea repos) V
readings.en: they remembered the blood of John their brother
readings.plain: They remembered the blood of their brother John

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. "The blood of" may have been added from 9:42 ("vengeance for their brother's blood"), which already makes plain that John was killed; a corrector of Sinaiticus struck the words out and then restored them. The KJV, like A, has only "remembered John their brother".

t: The marsh, or the mountain, of the Jordan?
p: Alexandrinus says "the mountain of the Jordan"; Sinaiticus says "the marsh", which fits 9:45. The Plain English Translation follows Sinaiticus.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), in Swete's notes; KJV ("the marsh of Jordan")
readings.en: the marsh of the Jordan

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Venetus (V) has no different reading in Swete's notes
readings.en: to the mountain of the Jordan

readings.w: Vulgate (ad ripam Jordanis), Douay
readings.en: to the bank of the Jordan

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. The Jordan valley has no mountain by that name, and the next battle is fought in the Jordan's "marsh and thicket" (9:45, ἕλος, the word Sinaiticus has here). ὄρος and ἕλος differ in only two letters, so the change is easy for a scribe.

p: A corrector of Sinaiticus and Venetus give three thousand of Bacchides' men killed.

readings.w: Swete's text (which he follows here; see the note); KJV; Vulgate (mille viri)
readings.en: about a thousand men

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V); Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a, the numeral γ´ = 3,000), in Swete's notes
readings.orig: χιλιους) ?? ℵ* γ ℵc.a τρισχιλιους V
readings.en: about three thousand

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text with the KJV and the Latin. Numbers are easily changed in copying, especially when written as letters, as Sinaiticus writes them. Swete's note on this verse reads "και διεπεσαν] κ. διεβησαν A επεσον δε ℵV": it reports διέβησαν "(they) crossed over" as Alexandrinus's reading where his text has διέπεσαν "fell", and ἔπεσον "fell" in Sinaiticus and Venetus. "Fell" is the sense all the editions follow.
b: The digitized note prints the first hand of Sinaiticus as "??": the sign it had is lost in the digital copy.

p: Alexandrinus has "they"; Sinaiticus and Venetus have "he", meaning Bacchides, as the KJV says.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Καὶ ἀπέστρεψαν εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ, καὶ ᾠκοδόμησαν
readings.en: and they returned to Jerusalem and built

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; KJV ("returned Bacchides")
readings.en: he returned

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. Either way the builders are Bacchides and his army, as 10:12 says ("the fortresses Bacchides had built"). The KJV names Bacchides, following the singular.

p: Alexandrinus has "the city and Beth-zur"; the KJV and the Latin make it one place, "the city Beth-zur".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: they fortified the city and Beth-zur

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), in Swete's notes
readings.orig: και Βεθσ.] της Βεθσ. τ. εν Βαιθσουρα V
readings.en: the city of Beth-zur, the one in Beth-zur

readings.w: Vulgate (civitatem Bethsuram), Douay; KJV ("the city Bethsura")
readings.en: he fortified the city Bethsura

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. "The city" alone usually means Jerusalem in 1 Maccabees, but Jerusalem was not held by Bacchides, only its Citadel, which is named separately; so many readers take "the city" here as Beth-zur itself, as the Latin and the KJV do. The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek and leaves the question open (see the note).

p: Alexandrinus has "they were angry"; Venetus and a corrector of Sinaiticus have "he", as the KJV does.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and they were angry with fury

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V) and Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (iratus); KJV
readings.orig: ωργισθησαν] ωργισθη εν ℵc.a ωργισθη V
readings.en: he was angry

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. "They" are most likely Bacchides and his army, angry at the renegades who had talked them into a failed campaign; the verse goes on "he decided to go back". In every copy the killing ("they killed") is plural.

p: The Greek gives the title Epiphanes to Alexander; the KJV gives it to his father Antiochus.

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, with Sinaiticus and Venetus, which differ only in the date)
readings.orig: Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ τοῦ Ἀντιόχου ὁ Ἐπιφανής
readings.en: Alexander, the (son) of Antiochus, the Epiphanes (Epiphanes in the nominative, agreeing with Alexander)

readings.w: KJV (1611), translating the same Greek; Vulgate (qui cognominatus est Nobilis)
readings.en: Alexander, the son of Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes

why: This is a difference of translation, not of text. In the Greek, "the Epiphanes" is in the nominative case and so belongs to Alexander, and Alexander Balas's own coins call him Epiphanes. The KJV attaches it to Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the father Alexander claimed. The Latin, "who was surnamed the Noble", can be read either way.

t: Authority for him or for them?
p: Alexandrinus says the king gave "them" (Jonathan and his people) authority; Sinaiticus and Venetus say "him".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: the king had given them authority

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (dedit ei); KJV ("given him authority")
readings.en: had given him authority

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. "Him" agrees with 10:6, where the authority is given to Jonathan, and may be a correction toward it; "them" makes the whole Jewish force the danger the Citadel feared.

p: In Alexandrinus "they" gave the hostages back to their parents; in Sinaiticus and the KJV, "he", Jonathan.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπέδωκαν αὐτοὺς τοῖς γονεῦσιν αὐτῶν
readings.en: and they gave them back to their parents

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (reddidit); KJV ("he delivered them")
readings.en: and he gave them

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. With "they", the Citadel's men themselves send the boys home; with "he", Jonathan does. The singular is the easier reading, since Jonathan is the hero of the scene.

p: Sinaiticus and Venetus describe the stones for Zion's wall as "four-foot" stones.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete (the last letters written over an erasure by a later hand, Aᵃ)
readings.en: of squared stones

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as first written (ℵ*) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes
readings.orig: τετραγωνων (γων sup ras Aa)] τετραποδων ℵ*V -πεδων ℵc.b
readings.en: of four-foot stones

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. "Squared stones" (ashlar) is the usual phrase for fine wall building. But the ending of A's word was rewritten over an erasure, so A's first hand may have had "four-foot", like ℵ and V.

a: Demetrius's army fled, and Alexander chased him
p: Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus as first written say Alexander's army fled and Demetrius gave chase.

readings.w: Swete's text, from Venetus and the correctors of Sinaiticus (ℵc.a); Vulgate; KJV
readings.orig: ἔφυγεν ἡ παρεμβολὴ Δημητρίου, καὶ ἐδίωξεν αὐτὸν ὁ Ἀλέξανδρος
readings.en: the army of Demetrius fled, and Alexander pursued him
readings.plain: Demetrius's army fled, and Alexander chased him

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Sinaiticus as first written (ℵ*), in Swete's notes
readings.orig: Δημητριου] Αλεξανδρου ℵ* (Δημ. ℵc.a c.b) A … o Αλεξανδρος] ο Δημητριος ℵ* (Αλεξανδρος ℵc.a) A
readings.en: the army of Alexander fled, and Demetrius pursued him
readings.plain: Alexander's army fled, and Demetrius chased him

why: The Plain English Translation follows the text Swete prints, which here leaves Alexandrinus. The story ends with Demetrius dead (10:50), and the next verses have Alexander as victor, so the reading of ℵc and V is the natural one. But A and ℵ* may preserve the first stage of the battle: Josephus says that Demetrius's left wing routed the enemy and plundered their camp, while his right, where the king fought, was beaten, and Demetrius was killed in a swamp (Antiquities 13.59–61). If so, "overpowered them" in the same verse belongs to the end of the day.

p: Sinaiticus and Venetus, followed by the KJV, have Jonathan "clothed in purple", as in 10:62.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and him wrapped in fine linen

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (purpura); KJV
readings.en: clothed in purple

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. "Purple" repeats 10:62 and is the easier reading, so a scribe would be more likely to change "linen" to "purple" than the other way. A σινδών is a fine linen garment or wrap, the dress of a wealthy man.

t: A governor, or a "partaker of his dominion"?
p: The Greek title is meridarch, a provincial governor; the KJV renders it as a sharer in the king's rule.

readings.w: Swete's text (all Greek copies)
readings.en: made him general and meridarch (governor of a district, a meris)

readings.w: KJV (1611), following the Latin; Vulgate (participem principatus), Douay
readings.en: made him a duke, and partaker of his dominion

why: This is a difference of translation. μεριδάρχης is a Seleucid title for the governor of a meris, a district or province; the word is formed from meris "part" and archē "rule", which the Latin rendered as "sharer in the rule". The KJV follows the Latin. Jonathan's appointment made him the king's own governor of Judea.

a: and those who had fled into it
p: Alexandrinus repeats "its temple"; the corrected Sinaiticus and Venetus say "those who had fled into it". The Plain English Translation follows them.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a, ℵc.b) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate; KJV
readings.orig: και τους συνφευγοντας (-φυγ. V) εις αυτο ℵc.a c.ᵇV
readings.en: and those who had fled together into it
readings.plain: and those who had fled into it

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν Δαγὼν καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν αὐτῆς ἐνεπύρισεν
readings.en: and the temple of Dagon and its temple he burned

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. A's "the temple of Dagon and its temple" says the same thing twice, while the people who fled into Beth-dagon (10:83) are counted among "those who were burned" (10:85). Sinaiticus's first scribe garbled the phrase (Swete: "τους συνφυτου | τουντας"), and its correctors and Venetus give the clear form. The Latin (et omnes qui fugerunt in illud) and the KJV agree.

p: Sinaiticus and Venetus, with the Latin and the KJV, add "to Jerusalem".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπέστρεψεν Ἰωναθὰν σὺν τοῖς παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἔχοντες σκῦλα πολλά
readings.en: and Jonathan returned with those with him, having much plunder

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (in Jerusalem); KJV
readings.en: returned to Jerusalem
readings.plain: returned to Jerusalem, loaded with plunder

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. The added words are natural, since Jonathan's base was Jerusalem (10:10), and they may have come in from formulas like 11:7 and 11:74.
b: Swete's note at this point is partly garbled in the digital copy ("ℵ7 Ιωναθαν] + ις (εις ℵc.a Ιηλμ ℵ"); the Venetus reading is clear.

p: The KJV's text reads "into Spain", a slip for Syria; every Greek and Latin witness has Syria.

readings.w: Swete's text (all Greek copies); Vulgate (in Syriam)
readings.en: and he went out into Syria

readings.w: King James Version (as printed in this site's KJV text); its source is not identified, and no Greek or Latin witness has it
readings.en: took his journey into Spain

why: "Spain" makes no sense: Ptolemy marches north along the coast through Azotus and Joppa (11:4–6). The KJV wording is an error in the English, not a Greek reading.

p: Ptolemy was Alexander's father-in-law (10:58); the KJV says "brother in law".

readings.w: Swete's text (all Greek copies); Vulgate (socer suus)
readings.en: because he was his father-in-law

readings.w: KJV (1611); its source is not identified
readings.en: because he was his brother in law

why: πενθερός means father-in-law, and Ptolemy had given Alexander his daughter Cleopatra (10:57–58). The KJV's "brother in law" is a mistranslation.

p: Alexandrinus reads "the towns of Ptolemais"; the first hand of Sinaiticus, the Latin and the KJV read "Ptolemy". The Plain English Translation follows them.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as first written (ℵ*), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (introiret civitatem Ptolemæus); KJV
readings.en: as Ptolemy entered the cities

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a)
readings.orig: ὡς δὲ εἰσεπορεύετο εἰς τὰς πόλεις Πτολεμαίδος
readings.en: as he entered the cities of Ptolemais
readings.plain: as he entered the towns of Ptolemais

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. "The towns of Ptolemais" is a phrase found nowhere else; the verse needs a subject, and Ptolemy is the subject of the whole passage. The names Πτολεμαῖος and Πτολεμαΐς differ by a letter or two and are confused elsewhere in the manuscripts.

p: Alexandrinus says "Alexander's face was changed"; other copies say Ptolemy changed toward Alexander, or that it was made known to him.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and the face of Alexander was changed

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), in Swete's notes
readings.en: and he was changed toward Alexander

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), in Swete's notes
readings.orig: ηλλ. το προσ. Aλεξανδρου] εδηλωθη τω Αλεξανδρω ℵ
readings.en: and it was made known to Alexander
readings.plain: It was made known to Alexander

readings.w: KJV ("and forsook Alexander"); Vulgate (alienavit se ab Alexandro)
readings.en: and he turned away from Alexander

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. A face that "changed" is a Hebrew way of speaking of a change of mood or favor (compare Daniel 3:19, where the Aramaic says the "image of his face" changed toward the three men). In A it may mean that Alexander grew hostile, or, as V and the Latin take it, that Ptolemy's favor toward Alexander changed. The other readings smooth the phrase.

t: "And they were named in his kingdom"
p: Sinaiticus as first written, and the Latin, add that the Jews became famous in the kingdom.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐνώπιον πάντων τῶν ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ
readings.en: before all those in his kingdom

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as first written (ℵ*, struck out by a corrector), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (et nominati sunt in regno), Douay
readings.orig: αυτου] + και ωνομασθησαν εν τη βασιλεια αυτου ℵ* (improb ℵc.a)
readings.en: and they were named in his kingdom
readings.plain: of everyone in his kingdom, and they became famous in his kingdom

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus. The extra clause repeats the sense of the one before it; a corrector of Sinaiticus struck it out. Its presence in the Latin shows that it circulated early.

p: Alexandrinus has "the plain of Nasor"; Sinaiticus and the Latin have "Asor", that is Hazor. The Plain English Translation follows them.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (in campo Asor), Douay
readings.en: the plain of Asor

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Venetus (V) has no different reading in Swete's notes; KJV ("the plain of Nasor")
readings.en: to the plain of Nasor

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. No place called Nasor is known, while Hazor, the old Canaanite city of Joshua 11, lies on the plain north of the Sea of Galilee, on the road from Gennesar to Kedesh (11:73). The N most likely came from the last letter of the word before it, πεδίον "plain", copied twice. Swete's note lacks its usual "]" after the lemma in the digital copy.

t: "Son of Absalom" or "son of the psalm singer"?
p: Sinaiticus turns Absalom into "the psalm singer", a scribe's misreading of a similar Greek word.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: Mattathias, the (son) of Absalom

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), in Swete's notes (the lemma is misspelled in the digital copy)
readings.orig: ο του Aφαλωμου] του ψαλμωδου ℵ
readings.en: (son) of the psalm singer
readings.plain: Mattathias son of the psalm singer

why: The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus, with the Latin (filius Absolomi) and the KJV. Ἀψαλώμου and ψαλμῳδοῦ look alike, and ℵ's reading is a copying slip. An Absalom appears again as the father of another Jonathan at 13:11.

a: with the noise of the armies
t: The ground shook from the armies, or at their noise?
p: Alexandrinus says the ground shook "from their armies"; Sinaiticus and Venetus add "the noise". The Plain English Translation follows them.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (a voce exercituum); KJV ("at the noise of the armies")
readings.orig: εσεισθη] εσαλευθη ℵV των παρεμβ. pr της φωνης ℵV | om αυτων ℵV
readings.en: the ground was shaken at the noise of the armies
readings.plain: with the noise of the armies

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐσείσθη ἡ γῆ ἀπὸ τῶν παρεμβολῶν αὐτῶν
readings.en: the ground shook from their armies

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. Both readings mean much the same, but ℵ and V, with the Latin, make the cause explicit: the trumpets of 9:12. A's shorter text may have lost τῆς φωνῆς by a slip, or ℵV may have added it; the sense of the scene favors the fuller reading, and the Plain English Translation follows it.

p: Alexandrinus spells the cistern's name Asphal; Sinaiticus and Venetus have Asphar, as do the Latin and the KJV.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (lacus Asphar); KJV
readings.en: Asphar

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: Asphal

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus in spelling. Λ and Ρ are easily confused, and the name is otherwise unknown; the Plain English Translation follows the majority of witnesses, which the Latin shares (lacus Asphar).

t: He could not, or they could not?
p: Alexandrinus has the singular, "he could not" (Bacchides, or "it could not be done"); Sinaiticus and Venetus have "they could not".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Venetus (V), in Swete's notes; Vulgate (sed non potuerunt); KJV ("howbeit they could not")
readings.en: and they were not able

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and he was not able (or: it could not be done)
readings.plain: But it could not be done

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. The plural fits the sentence, where the allies are the ones told to seize Jonathan, and the reason given, "their plot became known", is theirs. A's singular may refer to Bacchides or be impersonal; the difference is who failed, not what happened.
